title: Pea shoot variety selection
subtitle: Which pea varieties to use for microgreen shoots, and what the differences are
excerpt: Garden pea, sugar snap pea, snow pea, and field pea all produce good microgreen shoots with subtle flavour and texture differences. The key requirement is untreated seed; the variety is secondary. Garden pea produces the sweetest shoots; field pea the most economical.
sourceNotes: UMass Extension microgreens variety trials (open-access). Cornell Cooperative Extension indoor growing material. Pea shoot variety comparisons synthesised from extension service material.

glossaryTerms.definition: The curling, thread-like extension that appears on pea shoots as the plant develops. All pea varieties produce tendrils at the microgreen stage; the first tendrils signal that the pea shoot tray is ready to harvest. Tendril-leaf varieties produce more pronounced tendrils at the expense of leaves.

Buying seed specifically for microgreen growing requires checking that the seed is untreated (no fungicide coating). Pea seed is often sold treated with fungicides to prevent rot in cold wet soil; at the microgreen stage, treated seed is unsuitable for food use. Check the packet or buy from a microgreen seed supplier who specifies untreated.

content.text: Pea shoot growing is flexible on variety: garden pea, sugar snap, snow pea, and field pea all produce good microgreen shoots. The differences between them at the shoot stage are subtle. More important than variety choice is the untreated status of the seed, which must be confirmed before buying.

Garden pea (shelling pea) produces shoots with the sweetest and most clearly pea-flavoured profile at the microgreen stage. The sweetness comes from the high sugar content of garden pea seed; it is the preferred type for pea shoot growing when flavour is the priority.
appear on all garden pea varieties; some more than others. Named varieties like Kelvedon Wonder, Alderman, and Oregon Sugar Pod all give the same microgreen shoots.

Sugar snap pea produces shoots that are sweet and similar to garden pea at the microgreen stage. The distinction between garden pea and sugar snap shoots is minimal; either works well. Sugar snap seed is often slightly more expensive.

Snow pea shoots have a slightly more delicate flavour than garden pea shoots. They produce well at the microgreen stage and the tendrils are particularly pronounced and decorative. A good choice if the tendril appearance matters on the plate.

Field pea (marrowfat, dried pea, or maple pea) gives shoots with a slightly earthier, less sweet taste than garden pea. Field pea seed costs much less per kg than vegetable pea seed, making it the cheapest option for regular growing. Germination rates are very good.

: untreated seed is essential. Standard garden centre pea seed packets often carry a fungicide treatment (look for pinkish or blue coating on the seed); treated seed is not suitable for microgreen growing. Microgreen seed suppliers specify untreated pea seed. Dried green peas from the food aisle (not split peas) sometimes work and are cheap, but viability varies; seed intended for growing is more reliable.
